name: FiBA
tagline: Understanding invisible backdoors in collaborative learning
summary: A visually subtle trigger does not behave the same way in centralized and federated training. This study examines how limited local training, competing client updates, and server-side defenses affect invisible backdoor attacks, then investigates whether placing triggers in regions receiving little model attention changes attack success and detectability.

method.title: Evaluate invisible triggers
method.text: The study compares several invisible backdoor families with a visible-trigger baseline under federated training. Evaluation measures clean accuracy, attack success, and perceptual similarity.

method.title: Probe training and defenses
method.text: Experiments vary attacker participation and test server-side defenses, including robust aggregation and behavior detection. Distributed triggers and model replacement are also examined.

method.title: Study attention-based placement
method.text: Activation maps identify regions receiving less model attention. The paper evaluates placing LSB triggers in these regions and checks both attack success and detection by Neural Cleanse.

findings.title: Federation changes attack effectiveness
findings.text: Invisible attacks are generally less effective than the visible BadNet baseline in the reported experiments, but can still succeed with a minority of malicious clients. The tested defenses do not consistently mitigate them while preserving clean model accuracy.

findings.title: Higher success can mean easier detection
findings.text: On CIFAR-10, low-attention placement improves the reported LSB attack success rate, especially for the larger trigger. It also raises the Neural Cleanse anomaly score, exposing a tradeoff between attack effectiveness and detectability.

figure.source_label: Figure 1 in the accepted manuscript (PDF page 5)
figure.alt: Federated backdoor evaluation setup: honest and malicious clients train locally, with invisible triggers introduced at a malicious client and defenses applied during server aggregation.
figure.caption: Backdoor triggers enter during local training, while the server applies defenses when combining client updates. The study measures how this interaction shapes invisible attack success.

title: On the Effectiveness of Invisible Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of machine learning models across multiple devices, while preserving data privacy. However, it also introduces vulnerabilities to backdoor attacks, where malicious updates can corrupt the global model. This work focuses on the largely unexplored domain of Federated invisible Backdoor Attacks (FiBAs), which use visually indistinguishable triggers to manipulate model behavior without being detected. We investigate the feasibility and effectiveness of these attacks, considering the unique challenges posed by FL, such as limited local training time and the need for model update aggregation. Our study presents a comprehensive evaluation of the attack success rate (ASR) of invisible BAs under various settings and defenses. Based on our observations, we propose a backdoor trigger hiding technique based on low model attention regions to improve attack resilience in federated settings. Our findings provide critical insights into the optimization of invisible BAs in FL and highlights the need for robust defense mechanisms to safeguard FL systems.
